extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental physicists performing and interpreting fluid-resistance and wave-propagation experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental and theoretical methods for measuring fluid resistance and wave/pulse propagation using pendulums, immersed bodies, and comparisons across fluids. Includes practical setup notes, proportions and formula relations for deducing resistances and wave speeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sphere size (geometric progression) to extrapolate behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Globi sumantur in proportione Geometrica, puta quorum diametri sint digitorum 4, 8, 16, 32; ex progressione experimentorum colligetur quid in Globis adhuc majoribus evenire debeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sphere diameters in geometric progression so that trends observed in experimental results can be extrapolated to predict behaviour for still larger spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce resistances from arc differences and oscillation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measured arcs of descent/ascent and numbers of oscillations in different media (air vs water) and apply proportional relations (arc difference proportional to lost motion; oscillation counts indicative of energy loss) to compute relative resistances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record arc amplitudes for initial and final swings and count oscillations until a given return point; apply the algebraic relations (as in the text's worked example equating expressions like A+C = 85½, 8A + 64C = 4280, etc.) to solve for resistance components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarge vessel relative to immersed body to avoid confinement artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments showed that a too-narrow box (arca nimis angusta) impeded the motion of water and increased measured resistance beyond the expected law (resistentia in aqua augebatur in ratione velocitatis plusquam duplicata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the containing vessel is sufficiently large compared to the immersed body; otherwise flow constriction around the body will distort measurements and may produce super-quadratic velocity dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect resistance approx. proportional to fluid density and square of velocity for rapidly moving bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex jam descriptis satis liquet resistentiam corporum celeriter motorum densitati Fluidorum in quibus moventur proportionalem esse quamproxime. ... part illa resistentiæ penduli in aqua, quæ esset ut quadratum velocitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the approximate proportionality R ∝ ρ × v^2 for bodies moving rapidly in sufficiently free fluid, but treat it as an empirical approximation not exact in all regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for regime-dependent deviations (vacuum/trailing-region effects increase resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If velocity grows so that the medium cannot rush in behind the body, leaving some vacuum, resistance may become ~three times larger than predicted by the simple rule (resistentia tandem evadet quasi triplo major).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and correct for high-velocity regimes where wake formation and inability of fluid to refill the trail (effective partial vacuum) significantly increase resistance above the quadratic law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare resistances across fluids by alternating immersions; ratio ≈ density ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: By alternately filling a vessel with mercury and water and letting the same pendulum oscillate in each, measured resistance of mercury to that of water came out ≈13–14:1, i.e. approximately the density ratio of mercury to water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same pendulum/body and alternate fluids under identical geometric/kinematic conditions; for most sufficiently fluid liquids and suitably large/fast bodies the measured resistance ratio approximates the fluids' density ratio (watch for vessel-size effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test internal vs external surface resistance with filled vs empty hollow body
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspend a hollow container (pyxis) and compare oscillation times when empty and when filled with metal, correcting for added mass and air buoyancy; found internal resistance (in the cavity) negligible compared to external surface resistance (computed ratio A to B ≈ 5928:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully weigh empty and filled container and include the weight of displaced air; keep pendulum length constant; ensure suspension point is rigid; use the observed change in oscillation counts to infer internal-part resistance vs surface resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure suspension point/hook rigidity to avoid spurious retardation
rubrics_metrics.description: An earlier run with a weak hook (uncus infirmus) yielded faster retardation because the hook bent under the weight; replacing it with a firm hook made results agree with expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sufficiently rigid suspension so the point of suspension remains effectively immobile; otherwise flexing introduces systematic error in measured oscillation times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pendulums (including circular pendulums) for accurate measurement of resistance and velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendulums' motions are convenient to observe and measure; circular pendulum revolutions (measuring radii of first and last revolution) permit inference of initial and final velocities and thus of resistive losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pendulum setups for repeatable kinematics; measure radii/circle sizes or arc amplitudes and relate loss of velocity per revolution or per set of oscillations to resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model pressure propagation as non-rectilinear where particle alignment absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressio non propagatur per Fluidum secundum lineas rectas, nisi ubi particulæ Fluidi in directum jacent. When pressure reaches particles not collinear, it diverges and propagates obliquely in ever-widening fashion; obstacles cause spread around them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or designing experiments/theory about pressure transmission, account for divergence around oblique particle configurations and for conical/ frustum-like propagation rather than simple straight-ray transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect wave/pulse propagation to spread laterally and occupy immobile regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus omnis per Fluidum propagatus divergit a recto tramite in spatia immota. Wave motions (e.g., surface waves or pulses) dilate laterally and fill regions not initially in the direct path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically observe lateral dilation (e.g., water surface waves, sound through windows); do not assume motion propagates only along straight rays through an aperture—account for lateral expansion into the surrounding medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: In elastic media, particles execute reciprocal small oscillations governed by the pendulum law; number of pulses equals source vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne tremulum in Medio Elastico propagabit motum pulsuum undique in directum; singulæ Fluidi particulæ, motu reciproco brevissimo euntes & redeuntes, accelerantur semper & retardantur pro lege oscillantis Penduli. The number of propagated pulses equals the number of source vibrations and pulses do not multiply in transit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model particle motion in elastic media as small reciprocating oscillations with the same temporal law as a pendulum; when predicting pulse train structure, use one-to-one correspondence between source vibrations and propagated pulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulse speed depends on medium elasticity and density (composite square-root relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulsuum in Fluido Elastico propagatorum velocitates sunt in ratione composita ex dimidiata ratione vis Elasticæ directe & dimidiata ratione densitatis inverse; i.e. v ∝ sqrt(elasticity / density) (under assumption elasticity ∝ condensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing wave/pulse speeds in an elastic medium, use the square-root dependence on the ratio of elastic restoring force to density (modulo assumptions about linear elasticity and small amplitudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine wave velocity experimentally via a pendulum matched to wave latitudinal dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituatur Pendulum cujus longitudo ... æquetur latitudini Undarum: & quo tempore pendulum illud oscillationes singulas peragit, eodem Undæ progrediendo latitudinem suam propemodum conficient. (Prop. XLVI, XLIX.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a pendulum whose effective length relates to the wave's transverse measure; use the pendulum's oscillation period (one or two oscillations as specified) to infer the time the wave takes to traverse its own transverse dimension, thereby obtaining wave speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave speed scales inversely with square root of transverse dimension (latitudinum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLV: Undarum velocitas est in dimidiata ratione latitudinum. Corol. 2: undarum majorum vel minorum velocitas augebitur vel diminuetur in dimidiata ratione latitudinis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For water-surface undulations in which vertical motion approximates circular/rectilinear ascent/descent, expect larger transverse wavelengths to correspond to lower speeds per the stated square-root scaling (approximate relation; cycloidal corrections noted).
